bridges.statement: Multiple philosophical, scientific, moral, historical, and experiential considerations jointly support that God exists.
Contingent spacetime reality requires a necessary transcendent personal explanation.
A universe with an absolute beginning requires a timeless, spaceless, powerful personal cause.
Objective moral values require a divine foundation beyond evolutionary or social convention.
The resurrection best explains the central historical facts and evidences divine intervention.
The possibility of a maximally great being entails its actual and necessary existence.
Direct experience can rationally ground knowledge of God apart from public argument.
Natural accounts fit the world without God, while expected divine evidence is absent.
Missing observable effects that an active God should produce is evidence that God does not exist.
Physics supplies plausible natural cosmic origins and does not establish an absolute beginning.
Nonbelief and extensive suffering conflict with an available, powerful, morally good God.
Human moral knowledge and objective codes can develop naturally without divine grounding.
Biological imperfection and evolved complexity fit unguided processes rather than design.
Dependence of consciousness on brains and successful material models count against immaterial souls.

sections.title: Modal possibility and ultimate explanation
sections.rationale: Craig’s modal and contingency arguments are tested against Stenger’s objections concerning logic, observation, and explanatory premises.

sections.title: Cosmic beginning, laws, and natural origin
sections.rationale: Both speakers repeatedly contest beginnings, vacuum states, zero energy, quantum models, complexity, and causal explanation.

sections.title: Objective morality and natural development
sections.rationale: Craig’s grounding inference is answered through evolved and social morality, then revisited directly in rebuttal and closing.

sections.title: Jesus, sources, and resurrection
sections.rationale: The empty tomb, appearances, disciples, gospel reliability, and scholarly disagreement form a distinct historical exchange.

sections.title: Mind, experience, and epistemic reliability
sections.rationale: Brain dependence, direct religious experience, materialist reasoning, and the reliability of naturalistic cognition are substantively addressed.

sections.title: Expected evidence, hiddenness, evil, and burdens
sections.rationale: Stenger’s governing absence criterion, Craig’s disclosure replies, closing burdens, hiddenness, and suffering contact the motion directly.
